prompt: Let $f(x,y)=\ln(1-x^2-y^2)-\dfrac{1}{(y-x)^2}$ with domain $D=\{(x,y)\mid x\ne y,\ x^2+y^2<1\}$. Find the maximum value $M$ of $f(x,y)$ over $D$. You have to show that $M\ge f(x,y)$ for every $(x,y)\in D$. Here $\ln(\cdot)$ is the natural logarithm function.

solutions.title: Fix $x^2+y^2$ first
solutions.body:
Put $r=x^2+y^2\in(0,1)$ (note $r>0$ because $x\ne y$). Since
$$(y-x)^2=x^2+y^2-2xy=2r-(x+y)^2\le 2r ,$$
we get, for every $(x,y)\in D$,
$$f(x,y)=\ln(1-r)-\frac{1}{(y-x)^2}\le \ln(1-r)-\frac{1}{2r}=:g(r),$$
with equality exactly when $x+y=0$.

Now maximize $g$ on $(0,1)$:
$$g'(r)=-\frac{1}{1-r}+\frac{1}{2r^2}=\frac{1-r-2r^2}{2r^2(1-r)}=\frac{(1-2r)(1+r)}{2r^2(1-r)} .$$
This is positive for $0<r<\frac12$ and negative for $\frac12<r<1$, so $g$ attains its maximum on $(0,1)$ at $r=\frac12$:
$$g(r)\le g\!\left(\tfrac12\right)=\ln\tfrac12-1=-1-\ln2 .$$
Hence $f(x,y)\le -1-\ln 2$ for all $(x,y)\in D$. The value is attained: at $(x,y)=(\frac12,-\frac12)\in D$ we have $1-x^2-y^2=\frac12$ and $(y-x)^2=1$, so $f=\ln\frac12-1$.

**Answer: $M=-1-\ln2$**

prompt: The radius of the base of a right circular cone is $1$. The vertex of the cone is $V$, and $P$ is a point on the circumference of the base. The length of $PV$ is $6$ and the midpoint of $PV$ is $M$. A piece of string is attached to $M$ and wound tightly twice round the cone finishing at $P$. What is the length of the string?

solutions.title: Unroll the cone twice
solutions.body:
Cut the cone along $VP$ and flatten it. The lateral surface becomes a circular sector with centre $V$ and radius $6$ (the slant height), and its arc has length equal to the base circumference $2\pi$, so the sector angle is $\dfrac{2\pi}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

A string going twice round the cone becomes, after unrolling, a curve in **two** such sectors placed side by side: a sector of angle $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ whose two bounding radii both represent the line $VP$. The string starts at $M$ on the first radius ($VM=3$) and ends at the copy $P_2$ of $P$ on the last radius ($VP_2=6$), the angle $\angle MVP_2$ being $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Unrolling preserves lengths, and a tight string is as short as possible, so it is the straight segment $MP_2$ (the segment stays inside the sector because the sector is convex, its angle $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ being less than $\pi$). By the law of cosines,
$$MP_2^2=3^2+6^2-2\cdot3\cdot6\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=9+36+18=63,$$
so the string has length $\sqrt{63}=3\sqrt7\approx7.94$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt7$**

prompt: Find the volume of the region which is common to the interiors of the three circular cylinders $y^2+z^2=1$, $z^2+x^2=1$ and $x^2+y^2=1$.

solutions.title: Use the symmetry and integrate over one sixteenth
solutions.body:
The region $K=\{y^2+z^2\le1,\ z^2+x^2\le1,\ x^2+y^2\le1\}$ is unchanged by changing the sign of any coordinate and by permuting the coordinates. The $8$ sign changes and the swap $x\leftrightarrow y$ cut it into $16$ congruent pieces, one of which is
$$K_0=K\cap\{x\ge y\ge0,\ z\ge0\}.$$
In $K_0$ we have $y\le x$, so $z^2+x^2\le1$ implies $y^2+z^2\le1$. Hence $K_0$ is the set of points with $(x,y)$ in
$$R=\{0\le y\le x,\ x^2+y^2\le1\}$$
and $0\le z\le\sqrt{1-x^2}$. The region $R$ is bounded by $y=0$, $y=x$ and the circle; the line meets the circle at $x=\frac1{\sqrt2}$. Therefore
$$\operatorname{vol}(K_0)=\int_0^{1/\sqrt2}\!\!\int_0^{x}\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dy\,dx+\int_{1/\sqrt2}^{1}\!\!\int_0^{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dy\,dx
=\int_0^{1/\sqrt2}x\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx+\int_{1/\sqrt2}^1(1-x^2)\,dx .$$
Now
$$\int_0^{1/\sqrt2}x\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx=\Big[-\tfrac13(1-x^2)^{3/2}\Big]_0^{1/\sqrt2}=\frac13-\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}=\frac13-\frac{1}{6\sqrt2},$$
$$\int_{1/\sqrt2}^1(1-x^2)\,dx=\Big[x-\tfrac{x^3}{3}\Big]_{1/\sqrt2}^1=\frac23-\frac1{\sqrt2}+\frac{1}{6\sqrt2}.$$
Adding: $\operatorname{vol}(K_0)=1-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$. Hence
$$\operatorname{vol}(K)=16\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)=16-8\sqrt2\approx4.686 .$$

**Answer: $16-8\sqrt2$**

solutions.title: Slice by horizontal planes
solutions.body:
Fix $z\in[-1,1]$ and put $c=\sqrt{1-z^2}$. The slice at height $z$ is
$$\{|x|\le c,\ |y|\le c,\ x^2+y^2\le1\}.$$

- If $|z|\ge\frac1{\sqrt2}$, then $c\le\frac1{\sqrt2}$, the square $[-c,c]^2$ lies inside the unit disk, and the area is $4c^2=4(1-z^2)$.
- If $|z|<\frac1{\sqrt2}$, then $c>\frac1{\sqrt2}$ and the slice is the unit disk minus the four circular segments cut off by the lines $x=\pm c$, $y=\pm c$. These segments are disjoint (a point with $|x|>c$ and $|y|>c$ has $x^2+y^2>2c^2>1$). A segment cut off by a chord at distance $c$ from the centre has area $\arccos c-c\sqrt{1-c^2}$, and here $\arccos c=\arcsin|z|$, $\sqrt{1-c^2}=|z|$. So the area is
$$\pi-4\arcsin|z|+4|z|\sqrt{1-z^2}.$$

With $s=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ (so $s^3=\frac s2$, $\arcsin s=\frac\pi4$, $\sqrt{1-s^2}=s$), using symmetry in $z$:
$$\frac{V}{2}=\int_0^{s}\big(\pi-4\arcsin z+4z\sqrt{1-z^2}\big)\,dz+\int_s^1 4(1-z^2)\,dz .$$
The pieces are
$$\int_0^s\pi\,dz=\pi s,\qquad \int_0^s\arcsin z\,dz=\Big[z\arcsin z+\sqrt{1-z^2}\Big]_0^s=\frac{\pi s}{4}+s-1,$$
$$\int_0^s z\sqrt{1-z^2}\,dz=\frac13-\frac{s^3}{3}=\frac13-\frac s6,\qquad \int_s^1(1-z^2)\,dz=\frac23-s+\frac{s^3}{3}=\frac23-\frac{5s}{6}.$$
Hence
$$\frac V2=\pi s-\pi s-4s+4+\frac43-\frac{2s}{3}+\frac83-\frac{10s}{3}=8-8s,$$
so $V=16-16s=16-8\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $16-8\sqrt2$**

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $P$ be a point on $AB$. Suppose $\angle BAC=70^\circ$, $\angle APC=60^\circ$, $AC=\sqrt3$ and $PB=1$. Prove that $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle.
answer: $BA=BC$: from the sine rule $AP=2\sin50^\circ$, and $\sqrt3=2(1+2\sin50^\circ)\cos70^\circ$, i.e. $AC=2\,AB\cos70^\circ$ (equivalently $\angle ABC=40^\circ$).

solutions.title: Law of sines and law of cosines
solutions.body:
We show $AB=BC$.

In triangle $APC$ the angles are $\angle A=70^\circ$, $\angle P=60^\circ$, hence $\angle ACP=50^\circ$. By the law of sines,
$$\frac{AP}{\sin50^\circ}=\frac{AC}{\sin60^\circ}=\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt3/2}=2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad AP=2\sin50^\circ,\quad AB=AP+PB=1+2\sin50^\circ .$$
By the law of cosines in triangle $ABC$,
$$BC^2=AB^2+AC^2-2\,AB\cdot AC\cos70^\circ ,$$
so $BC=AB$ if and only if $AC^2=2\,AB\cdot AC\cos 70^\circ$, i.e. $AC=2\,AB\cos70^\circ$, i.e.
$$\sqrt3=2(1+2\sin50^\circ)\cos70^\circ .$$
Using $2\sin a\cos b=\sin(a+b)+\sin(a-b)$,
$$4\sin50^\circ\cos70^\circ=2\big(\sin120^\circ+\sin(-20^\circ)\big)=\sqrt3-2\sin20^\circ ,$$
and $2\cos70^\circ=2\sin20^\circ$. Hence $2(1+2\sin50^\circ)\cos70^\circ=2\sin20^\circ+\sqrt3-2\sin20^\circ=\sqrt3$, as needed. So $BA=BC$ and the triangle is isosceles. ∎

solutions.title: Find the angle at $B$
solutions.body:
As above, $\angle ACP=50^\circ$, and by the law of sines in $APC$, $PC=\dfrac{AC\sin70^\circ}{\sin60^\circ}=2\sin70^\circ$.

In triangle $BPC$: $PB=1$, $PC=2\sin70^\circ$ and $\angle BPC=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$. Let $\beta=\angle PBC$; then $\angle PCB=60^\circ-\beta$ with $0<\beta<60^\circ$, and the law of sines gives
$$\frac{\sin(60^\circ-\beta)}{\sin\beta}=\frac{PB}{PC}=\frac{1}{2\sin70^\circ}=\frac{1}{2\cos20^\circ}.$$
The left side is strictly decreasing in $\beta\in(0^\circ,60^\circ)$ (numerator decreases, denominator increases, both positive), so there is at most one solution. And $\beta=40^\circ$ is a solution: $\dfrac{\sin20^\circ}{\sin40^\circ}=\dfrac{\sin20^\circ}{2\sin20^\circ\cos20^\circ}=\dfrac{1}{2\cos20^\circ}$.

Hence $\angle ABC=40^\circ$ and $\angle ACB=180^\circ-70^\circ-40^\circ=70^\circ=\angle BAC$, so $BA=BC$: the triangle is isosceles. ∎

prompt: Let $a_n$ be a sequence of positive numbers ($n=1,2,\dots$, $a_n\ne0$ for all $n$), and let $b_n=(a_1+\cdots+a_n)/n$, the average of the first $n$ numbers of the sequence. Suppose $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{a_n}$ is a convergent series. Prove that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{b_n}$ is also a convergent series.
answer: Compare with the increasing rearrangement $a^*_n$: $b_{2m},b_{2m+1}\ge a^*_m/2$, so $\sum1/b_n\le 1/b_1+4\sum 1/a_n$. (Sharper: $\sum 1/b_n\le2\sum1/a_n$ by Cauchy–Schwarz.)

solutions.title: Increasing rearrangement
solutions.body:
Since $\sum 1/a_n$ converges, $1/a_n\to0$, so for every $M>0$ only finitely many $n$ have $a_n<M$. Hence the terms can be listed in increasing order: there is a rearrangement $a^*_1\le a^*_2\le\cdots$ of the sequence $(a_n)$ (each value taken with its multiplicity), and $\sum 1/a^*_n=\sum1/a_n$ because rearranging a series of positive terms does not change its sum.

*Step 1.* For every $n$, $a_1+\cdots+a_n\ge a^*_1+\cdots+a^*_n$, because the right side is the sum of the $n$ smallest terms of the sequence. So $b_n\ge b^*_n:=(a^*_1+\cdots+a^*_n)/n$.

(Careful: one may **not** simply assume that $(a_n)$ itself is increasing, since $b_n$ depends on the order of the terms — Step 1 is what makes the reduction legitimate.)

*Step 2.* For $m\ge1$, using that $a^*$ is increasing,
$$b^*_{2m}\ge\frac{a^*_{m+1}+\cdots+a^*_{2m}}{2m}\ge\frac{m\,a^*_m}{2m}=\frac{a^*_m}{2},\qquad
b^*_{2m+1}\ge\frac{a^*_{m+1}+\cdots+a^*_{2m+1}}{2m+1}\ge\frac{(m+1)a^*_m}{2m+1}\ge\frac{a^*_m}{2}.$$

*Step 3.* Therefore, for every $N$,
$$\sum_{n=1}^{2N+1}\frac1{b_n}\le\frac1{b_1}+\sum_{m=1}^{N}\left(\frac{1}{b^*_{2m}}+\frac1{b^*_{2m+1}}\right)\le\frac1{b_1}+\sum_{m=1}^N\frac{4}{a^*_m}\le\frac1{a_1}+4\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{a_n}.$$
The partial sums of the positive series $\sum1/b_n$ are bounded, so it converges. ∎

solutions.title: Cauchy–Schwarz (a sharp bound)
solutions.body:
Let $S_n=a_1+\cdots+a_n$, so $\dfrac1{b_n}=\dfrac{n}{S_n}$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$\left(\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{k^2}{a_k}\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\right)\ge\left(\sum_{k=1}^n k\right)^2=\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4},$$
so
$$\frac{n}{S_n}\le\frac{4}{n(n+1)^2}\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{k^2}{a_k}.$$
Summing over $n\le N$ and exchanging the order of summation,
$$\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{n}{S_n}\le4\sum_{k=1}^N\frac{k^2}{a_k}\sum_{n=k}^{N}\frac{1}{n(n+1)^2}.$$
Now
$$\frac{1}{n(n+1)^2}=\frac{n}{n^2(n+1)^2}<\frac{n+\frac12}{n^2(n+1)^2}=\frac12\left(\frac1{n^2}-\frac1{(n+1)^2}\right),$$
so the inner sum telescopes to less than $\dfrac{1}{2k^2}$. Hence
$$\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{1}{b_n}<4\sum_{k=1}^N\frac{k^2}{a_k}\cdot\frac{1}{2k^2}=2\sum_{k=1}^N\frac1{a_k}\le2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{1}{a_k}.$$
The partial sums are bounded, so $\sum1/b_n$ converges (and its sum is at most $2\sum1/a_n$). ∎

prompt: Ten cats are sitting on ten fence posts, numbered $1$ through $10$ in clockwise order and encircling a pumpkin patch. The cat on post #1 is white and the other nine cats are black. At 9:45 p.m. the cats begin a strange sort of dance. They jump from post to post according to the following two rules, applied in alternation at one second intervals. Rule 1: each cat jumps clockwise to the next post. Rule 2: all pairs of cats whose post numbers have a product that is $1$ greater than a multiple of $11$ exchange places. At 10 p.m., just as the Great Pumpkin rises out of the pumpkin patch, the dance stops abruptly and the cats look on in awe. If the first jump takes place according to Rule 1 at 9:45:01, and the last jump occurs at 10:00:00, on which post is the white cat sitting when the dance stops? (The first few jumps take the white cat from post $1$ to posts $2,6,7,\dots$)

solutions.title: Permutations: a period of 16 jumps
solutions.body:
**The two rules as permutations of the posts.** Rule 1 sends post $p$ to $p+1$ (and $10\to1$). For Rule 2, the pairs $\{p,q\}$ with $pq\equiv1\pmod{11}$, $p\ne q$, are
$$\{2,6\}\ (12),\quad\{3,4\}\ (12),\quad\{5,9\}\ (45),\quad\{7,8\}\ (56);$$
posts $1$ and $10$ are their own inverses mod $11$ and stay put.

**One round = Rule 1 followed by Rule 2.** Following a cat on post $p$:
$$1\to2\to6,\quad 6\to7\to8,\quad8\to9\to5,\quad5\to6\to2,\quad2\to3\to4,\quad4\to5\to9,\quad9\to10\to10,\quad10\to1\to1 .$$
Also $3\to4\to3$ and $7\to8\to7$. So one round acts as the permutation $(1\ 6\ 8\ 5\ 2\ 4\ 9\ 10)(3)(7)$, which has order $8$. Hence the positions repeat every $8$ rounds, i.e. every $16$ jumps.

**Counting jumps.** From 9:45:01 to 10:00:00 there is one jump per second: $15\cdot60=900$ jumps. Since $900=16\cdot56+4$, the final position is the position after $4$ jumps: $1\to2\to6\to7\to8$.

**Answer: post $8$**

solutions.title: Follow the white cat for one cycle
solutions.body:
Only the white cat matters. Its posts after jumps $1,2,3,\dots$ (Rule 1 on odd jumps, Rule 2 on even jumps) are
$$2,6,\ 7,8,\ 9,5,\ 6,2,\ 3,4,\ 5,9,\ 10,10,\ 1,1,\ \dots$$
After $16$ jumps it is back on post $1$ with Rule 1 next, so the pattern repeats with period $16$. The $900$th jump is jump number $900-16\cdot56=4$ of a cycle, and after $4$ jumps the white cat is on post $8$.

**Answer: post $8$**
